questions.prompt: After compilation, what does the JVM signature of `suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): User` look like, and why?

choices.text: `fun fetchUser(id: String): Deferred<User>`, because the compiler wraps every suspend function body in an implicit `async` and hands back a `Deferred` for the caller to await
`fun fetchUser(id: String, cont: Continuation<User>): Any?`: it returns the result or `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`
`fun fetchUser(id: String): User`, spawning a new dedicated OS thread that blocks until the network call finishes and the result object is ready
`fun fetchUser(id: String, callback: (User) -> Unit): Unit`, a plain callback interface with no return value and no `Continuation` parameter at all

sources.claim: Every suspending function has an additional `Continuation` parameter; `suspend fun <T> CompletableFuture<T>.await(): T` becomes `fun <T> CompletableFuture<T>.await(continuation: Continuation<T>): Any?`, returning `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED` when it suspends.
sources.title: Kotlin Coroutines design proposal (KEEP)

questions.explanation: The compiler applies a continuation-passing-style transform. Every suspend function gets an extra `Continuation` parameter. The return type becomes `Any?`, because the function either returns its result directly or returns `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED` to signal that it suspended and will resume the continuation later. No thread is blocked (choice c), and there is no `Deferred`: that only comes from `async`.

questions.prompt: You create `val dbDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)` for a database driver. Which statement is true?

choices.text: It creates and owns a brand-new pool of 4 dedicated threads that you must explicitly shut down yourself when the driver is no longer needed
It guarantees that at most 4 coroutines exist at once, like a `Semaphore(4)` guarding the whole database driver's lifetime
A view reusing `Dispatchers.IO` threads: at most 4 run at once, uncounted against IO's own limit
It shares IO's 64-thread limit, so other IO work is capped at 60 threads while the view is busy running its own coroutines

sources.claim: The view reuses threads from the original dispatcher and does not constitute a resource; Dispatchers.IO is elastic, so views are not restricted by its capacity; pitfall: it limits parallel execution, not how many coroutines execute concurrently.
sources.title: limitedParallelism | kotlinx.coroutines API

sources.claim: Dispatchers.IO defaults to 64 threads or the number of cores (whichever is larger), and its limitedParallelism views are not restricted by the Dispatchers.IO parallelism.
sources.title: Dispatchers.IO | kotlinx.coroutines API

questions.explanation: `limitedParallelism` returns a view, not a resource. It reuses the original dispatcher's threads and does not need closing. `Dispatchers.IO` is elastic here: the parallelism of its views is not taken out of IO's own limit. So this is the recommended replacement for `newFixedThreadPoolContext(n)`. Choice b is the documented pitfall: the view limits how many coroutines run in parallel, not how many are running concurrently while suspended. For that, use a `Mutex` or `Semaphore`.

questions.prompt: A function runs on `Dispatchers.Default` and calls `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { readFile() }`. What typically happens to the thread?

choices.text: The coroutine is always moved to a brand-new dedicated IO thread pool, paying the full cost of a real context switch and a thread park/unpark cycle
The call throws `IllegalStateException`, because a coroutine on Default is not allowed to switch to the IO dispatcher
Nothing is dispatched at all: `withContext` here only renames the coroutine in the debugger, without touching any thread
IO shares threads with Default, so it usually stays on the same thread and only the parallelism accounting changes

sources.claim: Dispatchers.IO and its views share threads with the Default dispatcher, so `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` when already on Default typically does not lead to an actual switch to another thread.
sources.title: Dispatchers.IO | kotlinx.coroutines API

sources.claim: Kotlin optimizes switching between Dispatchers.Default and Dispatchers.IO to avoid thread switches whenever possible.
sources.title: Improve app performance with Kotlin coroutines

questions.explanation: `Dispatchers.IO` and its views share threads with `Dispatchers.Default`. Calling `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` from Default therefore usually does not move to another thread. The Android docs also say that Kotlin optimizes switching between Default and IO to avoid thread switches whenever possible. Switching to a dispatcher that does not share threads, such as `Main`, does cost a real dispatch there and another one back.

questions.prompt: Inside `viewModelScope.launch { ... }` a teammate writes `launch(Job()) { upload() }` so that the upload has its own Job. What is the effect?

choices.text: The new `Job()` overrides the parent Job: the upload is no longer a child, so it outlives `viewModelScope` uncancelled
Nothing changes: a coroutine always becomes a child of whatever scope its `launch` call was written inside, regardless of arguments
The upload becomes a supervisor child, so its failures do not cancel siblings, but it is still cancelled together with the ViewModel
It does not compile, because `Job()` is not a valid `CoroutineContext` element and cannot appear as a `launch` argument

sources.claim: When a different Job object is passed as the context for the new coroutine, it overrides the Job of the parent scope, so the coroutine is not a child; context elements are combined with the `+` operator.
sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: The context passed to `launch` is combined with the scope's context using `+`, and later elements win. Passing an explicit `Job` replaces the parent's Job. The docs call this out as one of the two ways to break the parent-child relationship, the other being a different scope such as `GlobalScope`. The coroutine then outlives the ViewModel. Choice c is the usual misunderstanding: it applies neither to `Job()` nor to `SupervisorJob()` passed this way.

questions.prompt: A helper `suspend fun show(text: String) = withContext(Dispatchers.Main.immediate) { label.text = text }` is called from both the main thread and background threads. What does `.immediate` change?

choices.text: It always runs the block synchronously on whatever thread calls it, main or background, skipping the handler entirely
It skips the re-dispatch when already on the main looper; other threads still dispatch to main as usual
It gives the block a higher priority slot in the main looper's message queue, ahead of pending input and draw messages
It makes the block non-cancellable, so that in-flight UI updates always finish even after the coroutine is cancelled

sources.claim: Dispatchers.Main.immediate executes coroutines immediately when already in the right context (current looper is the same as the handler's looper) without an additional re-dispatch; it is supported on Android.
sources.title: MainCoroutineDispatcher.immediate | kotlinx.coroutines API

questions.explanation: `Main.immediate` executes immediately, without an extra dispatch, when the caller is already in the right context (the current looper is the main looper). From other threads it dispatches normally. On main-thread paths this avoids posting a message and waiting a frame. Choice a would be unsafe, since it would touch views off the main thread. It is closer to what `Dispatchers.Unconfined` does.

questions.prompt: You decompile `suspend fun load() { val user = api.user(); val feed = api.feed(user.id); render(user, feed) }`. Explain the state machine the compiler generated: what the `label` field is, where `user` lives while suspended, how many states there are, and what happens when `api.user()` actually suspends.

sources.claim: The compiler creates only one class per suspending lambda with any number of suspension points; the state machine has a `label` field and stores locals as fields; the number of states is suspension points plus one; a suspending function returns `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED` when it suspends.
sources.title: Kotlin Coroutines design proposal (KEEP)

questions.explanation: Seniors can explain why suspension does not block a thread: the frame is unwound and its state lives on the heap. They also know that one class per function (not per suspension point) keeps the cost low.

model_answer.summary: The compiler generates one state-machine continuation class for the function. A `label` field records which suspension point to resume at, and locals such as `user` are saved in fields so they survive suspension. With two suspension points there are three states. When a callee returns `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`, the function returns that marker up the stack. The continuation's `resumeWith` later re-enters the function, and it jumps to the saved label.
key_points: The CPS transform adds a `Continuation` parameter and changes the return type to `Any?`
One state-machine class per suspend function or lambda, however many suspension points it has
`label` records the current state; locals that are needed after a suspension point (like `user`) are stored as fields of the state machine
Number of states = suspension points + 1, so this function has three states
When a callee returns `COROUTINE_SUSPENDED`, the function returns it immediately, freeing the thread; resuming the continuation re-enters the function at the saved label

questions.prompt: A code review finds `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` wrapped around nearly every repository call, including in-memory cache reads, and the ViewModel also wraps calls in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`. Explain what main-safety means, who should own the dispatcher switch, what `withContext` really costs, and how you would clean this up.

sources.claim: Suspend functions should be main-safe: a class doing long-running blocking operations is in charge of moving execution off the main thread using withContext; don't hardcode Dispatchers, inject them.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

sources.claim: withContext() does not add extra overhead compared to an equivalent callback-based implementation, and Kotlin optimizes switching between Default and IO to avoid thread switches whenever possible.
sources.title: Improve app performance with Kotlin coroutines

questions.explanation: The senior view is about ownership, not micro-optimisation. The class that blocks owns the switch, and it happens once. Seniors quote the real cost model rather than assuming each `withContext` is an expensive thread hop.

model_answer.summary: A suspend function should be main-safe: the class that does blocking work moves it off the main thread itself, so callers never pick dispatchers. `withContext` costs no more than an equivalent callback, and Default-to-IO switches usually avoid a thread change. Switching to a dispatcher that does not share threads still costs a dispatch there and back. So put the switch once, at the blocking boundary, with an injected dispatcher, and remove the redundant wrappers.
key_points: Main-safe means safe to call from the main thread; the class doing long-running blocking work is responsible for moving it off the main thread with `withContext`
Callers (the ViewModel) should not wrap calls again; wrapping pure in-memory work is unnecessary
`withContext` adds no extra overhead compared to an equivalent callback-based implementation, and Default/IO switches usually avoid a real thread switch
Switching to a dispatcher that does not share threads means extra dispatches: the block is scheduled on the new dispatcher and then goes back to the original one
Inject the dispatcher instead of hardcoding `Dispatchers.IO`, so tests can substitute a TestDispatcher

questions.prompt: Explain what a `CoroutineContext` is, name its main elements and what each controls, and describe how a child coroutine's context is built from its parent's when you call `launch(Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineName("sync"))`.

sources.claim: A CoroutineContext defines the behavior of a coroutine using Job (lifecycle), CoroutineDispatcher (threads), CoroutineName (debugging) and CoroutineExceptionHandler (uncaught exceptions).
sources.title: Improve app performance with Kotlin coroutines

sources.claim: A coroutine launched in the scope of another inherits its context and its Job becomes a child of the parent's job; elements are combined with `+`; GlobalScope or an explicit Job breaks the parent-child relationship.
sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: A senior answer treats the context as an indexed set in which the right-hand element wins. They know the Job is always new for each child, and they understand that this is how the structure is kept, and how it is accidentally broken.

model_answer.summary: A `CoroutineContext` is a set of elements that together define how a coroutine behaves: the Job (its lifecycle), the dispatcher (its threads), a CoroutineName (for debugging) and a CoroutineExceptionHandler (for uncaught exceptions). A child takes the parent scope's context, adds the elements passed to `launch` with `+` (they override matching elements), and gets a new Job that is a child of the parent's Job.
key_points: Elements: `Job` controls lifecycle and cancellation, `CoroutineDispatcher` picks the threads, `CoroutineName` names the coroutine for debugging, `CoroutineExceptionHandler` handles uncaught exceptions
Elements are combined with `+`; an element on the right replaces one of the same key
A child inherits the scope's context, and its new Job becomes a child of the parent's Job, so cancelling the parent cancels the children recursively
Passing a different scope (e.g. `GlobalScope`) or an explicit `Job` breaks the parent-child link
In debug mode the `CoroutineName` shows up in the thread name, which helps when reading logs

choices.text: Right after printing `launched`, since `launch` is fire-and-forget and returns to the caller without waiting
Never returns: `coroutineScope` blocks the calling thread forever waiting on the child's `Job.join()`
Only after the child completes: a parent always waits for all of its children
Immediately, with the child left detached and silently cancelled the moment the scope function returns

sources.claim: A parent coroutine always waits for the completion of all its children; a parent does not have to explicitly track the children it launches or use Job.join to wait for them.
sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: Structured concurrency means a parent coroutine always waits for all its children to complete, without an explicit `join`. `coroutineScope` returns only when its body and all its children are done. Choice a confuses "launch returns immediately" with "the scope returns immediately". The call to `launch` does return at once, but the scope that contains it does not.

choices.text: `profile` finishes normally and `feed.await()` returns null
The failure cancels the scope: `profile` is cancelled and `screen()` throws the `IOException`
Only `feed.await()` throws; `profile` keeps running and its result is kept
The exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler and the app crashes, whatever the caller catches

sources.claim: With async inside coroutineScope, if the code throws an exception, all the coroutines launched in its scope are cancelled, and the exception propagates.
sources.title: Composing suspending functions | Kotlin Documentation

sources.claim: If a coroutine encounters an exception other than CancellationException, it cancels its parent with that exception.
sources.title: Coroutine exceptions handling | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: In `coroutineScope`, a child that fails with a non-cancellation exception cancels its parent scope, which cancels all other children, and the scope rethrows the exception to the caller. This is what you want for all-or-nothing parallel decomposition. Choice c describes `supervisorScope` combined with a `try`/`catch` around `feed.await()`.

questions.prompt: Inside `supervisorScope { launch { loadAds() }; launch { loadFeed() } }`, `loadAds()` throws. What happens?

choices.text: Both children are cancelled immediately and `supervisorScope` itself rethrows the exception to its caller
`supervisorScope` catches the failure and automatically retries `loadAds()` once before giving up
The exception is silently dropped, since supervision means no failure ever surfaces anywhere
`loadFeed()` keeps running; the ads exception is handled like a root coroutine's, via a `CoroutineExceptionHandler`

sources.claim: With supervision, a failure of a child does not propagate to the supervisor or its other children; supervisorScope cancels all its children only if it failed itself; coroutines launched directly inside supervisorScope use the CoroutineExceptionHandler installed in their scope like root coroutines do.
sources.title: Coroutine exceptions handling | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: Supervision is one-directional: a child's failure does not cancel the supervisor or its other children. `supervisorScope` cancels its children only if it fails itself. Each child must therefore handle its own exceptions. A child launched directly in `supervisorScope` uses the scope's `CoroutineExceptionHandler` the way a root coroutine does. Choice c is the dangerous assumption: without a handler the exception still reaches the platform's uncaught handler, which on Android crashes the app.

questions.prompt: In a Fragment you collect a Flow with `viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.items.collect { render(it) } }`. What is the gap, and what does the recommended API fix?

choices.text: It only cancels at Lifecycle destruction; collection keeps running while stopped. `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` starts/cancels it around STARTED/STOPPED
`lifecycleScope` is fully cancelled on every `onPause` call, so you silently miss events; switching the collector to `GlobalScope` restores them
`lifecycleScope` never cancels on its own; you must cancel the job manually yourself inside `onDestroyView`
There is no gap here at all: plain `collect` automatically pauses itself while the lifecycle state is below STARTED

sources.claim: Any coroutine launched in a LifecycleScope is canceled when the Lifecycle is destroyed; repeatOnLifecycle launches the block in a new coroutine every time the lifecycle is in the STARTED state and cancels it when it's STOPPED.
sources.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components (Views)

questions.explanation: A coroutine in `lifecycleScope` is cancelled only when the Lifecycle is destroyed. For a view, that is well after it has left the screen, so the collector keeps working while stopped. `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` launches the block each time the lifecycle reaches STARTED and cancels it at STOPPED. Choice d mixes this up with the older `launchWhenStarted`-style behaviour. Plain `collect` does not pause by itself.

questions.prompt: Bookmarking an article must complete even if the user leaves the screen right after tapping. Which design do the Android coroutine guidelines recommend?

choices.text: Launch the write in `viewModelScope`, because that scope survives configuration changes like a screen rotation
Use `GlobalScope.launch`, because nothing ever cancels a coroutine started on `GlobalScope`
Inject an external scope owned by a longer-lived object into the repository: `externalScope.launch { dataSource.bookmark(article) }.join()`
Wrap the write in `runBlocking` on the calling thread, so that the write cannot be interrupted or cancelled once it starts

sources.claim: For work that should outlive the screen, inject an external CoroutineScope and launch in it (`externalScope.launch { ... }.join()`); externalScope should be created and managed by a class that lives longer than the current screen, such as the Application class.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

questions.explanation: Work that must outlive the screen belongs in a scope that lives longer than the screen. The docs recommend injecting an `externalScope` created and managed by a longer-lived class, such as the Application or a ViewModel scoped to a navigation graph. The repository launches in it and `join`s, so the caller still waits while it is present. `viewModelScope` is cancelled when the user leaves. `GlobalScope` hardcodes the scope and cannot be controlled in tests. `runBlocking` would block the calling thread.

questions.prompt: A legacy codebase uses `GlobalScope.launch` for analytics, token refresh and screen data loading. Explain why `GlobalScope` is discouraged, which of these uses (if any) is acceptable, and what you would replace each one with on Android.

sources.claim: GlobalScope has no Job, so it is impossible to cancel or wait for its coroutines; it has no CoroutineExceptionHandler, so exceptions crash the application on Android; it is a delicate API for top-level coroutines not limited by structured concurrency.
sources.title: GlobalScope | kotlinx.coroutines API

sources.claim: Avoid GlobalScope: it promotes hard-coding values, makes testing very hard, and prevents having a common CoroutineContext for all coroutines built into the scope.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

questions.explanation: Seniors sort the uses by lifetime and move each one to the right owner, rather than just saying "never use GlobalScope". They know the Android-specific crash behaviour and point out that testability is the practical reason teams ban it.

model_answer.summary: `GlobalScope` has no Job. Nothing can cancel or wait for its coroutines, it has no exception handler, and it hardcodes a scope that tests cannot control. Screen loading belongs in `viewModelScope`. Work that must outlive a screen, like token refresh or analytics, belongs in an injected application-level scope with a `SupervisorJob` and an exception handler. Truly process-long background loops are the only documented `GlobalScope` use, and they require `@OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)`.
key_points: GlobalScope has no Job, so you cannot cancel or wait for its coroutines; work continues after the UI that needed it is gone, and suspended coroutines can leak resources
GlobalScope has no CoroutineExceptionHandler, so failures reach the platform's last-resort handling, which on Android crashes the app
It hardcodes the scope (and often the dispatcher), which makes testing hard and prevents a common context
Screen data belongs in `viewModelScope`, which is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared

Work that outlives screens goes in an injected application-scoped `CoroutineScope`; `GlobalScope` is a delicate API needing `@OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class)`, only for long-lived process-wide loops

questions.prompt: To stop one failing request from cancelling the others, a teammate changes `viewModelScope.launch { ... }` calls to `viewModelScope.launch(SupervisorJob()) { ... }`. Explain what this actually does to the Job hierarchy, the bugs it introduces, and the correct way to isolate failures.

sources.claim: When a different Job object is passed as the context for the new coroutine, it overrides the Job of the parent scope; when the parent coroutine is cancelled, all its children are recursively cancelled.
sources.title: Coroutine context and dispatchers | Kotlin Documentation

sources.claim: With SupervisorJob and supervisorScope, a failure or cancellation of a child does not propagate to the supervisor or its other children, and every child should handle its exceptions by itself.
sources.title: Coroutine exceptions handling | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: This is a classic senior trap. Candidates who understand context merging explain that `SupervisorJob()` passed to a builder becomes the parent of just that one coroutine, cut off from the scope. It does not turn the scope into a supervisor.

model_answer.summary: Passing a Job to `launch` replaces the parent Job in the new coroutine's context. The coroutine is no longer a child of `viewModelScope`: it is not cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, and nothing waits for it, so it leaks. It also does not give supervision to its siblings. To isolate failures, use `supervisorScope { }` inside the coroutine, or catch the exceptions in each child.
key_points: A new coroutine's Job is normally a child of the scope's Job; passing an explicit Job in the context overrides that parent
The coroutine now outlives the ViewModel: `onCleared` cancelling `viewModelScope` does not reach it, which is a leak and can update stale UI
The parent no longer waits for it, and its failure no longer reaches the parent, so the structure is broken instead of supervised
Correct isolation: wrap parallel children in `supervisorScope { }`, where a child's failure does not cancel its siblings, and handle each child's exceptions (try/catch or a handler)
Or catch expected exceptions (e.g. `IOException`) inside each launched block and turn them into UI state

questions.prompt: Design the constructor of an `ArticlesRepository` that loads data in parallel and also performs writes that must finish even if the screen closes. Explain which dependencies you inject and why, and how the design helps unit tests.

sources.claim: Inject Dispatchers; the data and business layers expose suspend functions and Flow; use coroutineScope or supervisorScope for work bound to the caller, and an injected externalScope for work that should outlive the screen; inject TestDispatchers in tests.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

sources.claim: If your class creates coroutines that don't complete on their own and should be canceled at the end of the test, inject TestScope.backgroundScope instead of the TestScope itself.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.explanation: Seniors decide which scope each piece of work lives in based on its lifetime. They inject both the dispatcher and the scope so the class can be tested deterministically, and they know the default-argument trick (`externalScope = GlobalScope` style) is only a stopgap.

model_answer.summary: Inject the data sources, a `CoroutineDispatcher` (instead of hardcoding `Dispatchers.IO`/`Default`) and an external application-scoped `CoroutineScope`. Parallel reads use `coroutineScope { async ... }`, so they follow the caller's lifecycle. Must-finish writes use `externalScope.launch { }.join()`. In tests you pass a TestDispatcher and a test scope that share one scheduler.
key_points: Inject dispatchers instead of hardcoding them, so tests can replace them with TestDispatchers
Expose suspend functions for one-shot calls and Flow for streams, so the caller controls lifecycle and cancellation
Use `coroutineScope`/`supervisorScope` with `async` for parallel work that should be cancelled with the caller
Inject an external scope created by a longer-lived owner (the Application, or a ViewModel scoped to a navigation graph) for work that must outlive the screen
In tests, inject a `TestDispatcher` (sharing the test scheduler) and, for coroutines that never finish, `TestScope.backgroundScope`

questions.prompt: `val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (line in hugeFile) parse(line) }` runs, where `parse` is a plain (non-suspending) function. You call `job.cancel()`. What happens?

choices.text: The loop stops at once: `cancel()` interrupts the underlying thread the same way `Thread.interrupt()` would
The loop keeps running to completion, since cancellation is cooperative and nothing here checks for it; add `ensureActive()`
The loop stops at the very next `parse` call, because every function call made from inside a coroutine checks for cancellation
`cancel()` throws `IllegalStateException` on the caller, because the targeted job is currently busy running work

sources.claim: Cancellation in coroutines is cooperative: when a coroutine's Job is cancelled, the coroutine isn't cancelled until it suspends or checks for cancellation; one way to check is to call ensureActive in the loop.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

questions.explanation: Cancelling a Job only marks it as cancelled. The code stops only when it suspends at a cancellable suspension point or checks for cancellation itself. A CPU loop of plain function calls does neither. Add `ensureActive()`, check `isActive`, or call `yield()` in the loop. Choice a is a Java-thread intuition: coroutines never interrupt threads on `cancel()`.

choices.text: `catch (e: Exception)` also catches `CancellationException`, so a cleared ViewModel shows Error instead of ending cancelled
`try`/`catch` simply does not work inside a launched coroutine body; you are required to install a `CoroutineExceptionHandler` instead
`repo.load()` exceptions are only ever delivered to a matching `await()` call, never to a `try`/`catch` written around a `launch` block like this
Setting `_state.value` from inside a coroutine is not thread-safe and can corrupt the `StateFlow`'s internal state

sources.claim: To enable coroutine cancellation, don't consume exceptions of type CancellationException (don't catch them, or always rethrow them if caught); prefer catching specific exception types like IOException over Exception or Throwable.
sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

sources.claim: CancellationException is thrown by cancellable suspending functions if the Job of the coroutine is cancelled while it is suspending; it indicates normal cancellation of a coroutine.
sources.title: CancellationException | kotlinx.coroutines API

questions.explanation: Suspending functions throw `CancellationException` when the coroutine is cancelled while suspended. That is normal cancellation, not an error. A catch-all `Exception` handler catches it too. The coroutine then treats cancellation as a failure and carries on as if it were still active. The Android guidance says: don't consume `CancellationException` (rethrow it if you catch it), and catch specific types like `IOException`. Choice b is false: `try`/`catch` is the normal way to handle errors in a coroutine.

choices.text: The handler on the inner `launch` logs it, and nothing else in the coroutine hierarchy is affected at all
The handler logs it, and the outer parent coroutine keeps running normally afterward
The child's handler is never used: it hands off to its parent, cancelling it, handled at the root
The exception is lost entirely, because nested `launch` calls silently swallow any exception thrown inside them

sources.claim: All children coroutines delegate handling of their exceptions to their parent coroutine, up to the root, so the CoroutineExceptionHandler installed in their context is never used; the handler is invoked only on uncaught exceptions.
sources.title: Coroutine exceptions handling | Kotlin Documentation

questions.explanation: `CoroutineExceptionHandler` is used only for uncaught exceptions at the root of the hierarchy, or in the direct children of a supervisor. A regular child delegates its exception to its parent, and so on up to the root, so a handler installed on the child is never used. The failure cancels the parent. This is the classic mistake of putting the handler in the wrong place. Install it on the scope or root coroutine, or use `try`/`catch` inside the child.

questions.prompt: What does `withTimeout(1.seconds) { Thread.sleep(10_000); fetch() }` do?

choices.text: It throws `TimeoutCancellationException` after exactly 1 second, because `withTimeout` interrupts the blocked thread the way `Thread.interrupt()` does
It quietly returns `null` after waiting exactly 1 second, without throwing anything at all
It never times out at all, because calling `Thread.sleep` inside the block disables the coroutine's timeout timer
`Thread.sleep` runs the full 10 seconds; timeouts cancel cooperatively at the next cancellable point

questions.prompt: Which claims describe NonCancellable cleanup and withTimeout? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use withContext(NonCancellable) for suspending cleanup in finally.
Launching a NonCancellable child preserves normal parent-child ownership.
NonCancellable is an always-active Job intended for withContext.
withTimeout guarantees a completed block result reaches the caller.
A timeout can fire after the block finishes but before its result is delivered.

questions.explanation: a is correct: The API documents this cleanup pattern. b is incorrect: Using it with launch breaks the parent-child relationship. c is correct: NonCancellable permits cleanup despite parent cancellation. d is incorrect: Timeout cancellation can race with delivery of the result. e is correct: The API explicitly documents this asynchronous timeout race.

sources.claim: NonCancellable is always active and intended for withContext cleanup; using it with launch breaks the parent-child relationship.

choices.text: Use runTest so delays on its test scheduler use virtual time.
Inject TestDispatchers that share the test scheduler.
Use Thread.sleep to advance runTest virtual time in retry assertions.
Use currentTime and scheduler controls to inspect backoff timing.
Expect delays on hardcoded Dispatchers.IO to be skipped by runTest.

questions.explanation: a is correct: runTest skips scheduler-controlled delays. b is correct: A shared scheduler coordinates all test dispatchers. c is incorrect: Sleeping advances wall-clock time rather than virtual time. d is correct: The scheduler exposes currentTime and advancement APIs. e is incorrect: Dispatchers.IO is outside the virtual-time scheduler.

sources.claim: runTest uses virtual time and scheduler controls for test-dispatcher delays, whereas delays running on Dispatchers.IO are not skipped.

questions.prompt: Which statements describe runBlocking in coroutine code? Select all that apply.

choices.text: runBlocking blocks the thread on which it is called until completion.
Calling runBlocking inside a suspend function releases its thread.
Calling runBlocking from suspend code can cause thread starvation.
runBlocking changes every blocking operation into a non-blocking one.
In suspend code, call a suspend function directly instead of bridging with runBlocking.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Blocking the caller is the defining behavior of runBlocking. b is incorrect: Inside suspend code it blocks instead of suspending. c is correct: Blocking scarce dispatcher threads can starve other work. d is incorrect: It is a blocking bridge, not a transformation of blocking calls. e is correct: The API warns that runBlocking in suspend functions is redundant.

sources.claim: runBlocking blocks the caller thread; using it inside a suspend function is redundant and can cause thread starvation.

questions.prompt: A tracker starts long-running collectors. Which choices give their lifetime a clear owner? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Tie its CoroutineScope to an entity and cancel it when that entity is destroyed.
Assume choosing Dispatchers.IO automatically cancels all running collectors as soon as the consumer screen closes.
Keep starting collectors without tracking or cancelling their Jobs.
Inject backgroundScope in tests for collectors that should be cancelled at test end.
Recognize that work continuing after its consumer disappears can leak resources.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Lifecycle ownership ensures no-longer-needed work is cancelled. b is incorrect: A dispatcher selects execution threads, not consumer lifetime. c is incorrect: Uncancelled long-running work can continue and retain resources. d is correct: TestScope.backgroundScope is cancelled automatically at test completion. e is correct: The GlobalScope API describes the resource-leak risk.

sources.claim: GlobalScope work is not tied to a consumer lifetime and can continue after destruction; cancel an entity-owned scope to avoid resource leaks.
